_about: Crop table for shelf-life and respiration. Edit freely. JSON has no comments, so every crop has a 'source' field. SL_ref_days is the storage life when kept at T_ref_C. Q10 = how many times faster quality is lost for every 10 C warmer. Q10 values are typical literature ranges (2-4 for fresh produce) and are APPROXIMATE - treat shelf-life output as an estimate, not a guarantee.

tomato.label: Tomato (firm-ripe)
tomato.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (2016), Tomato: firm-ripe 10-12 C for safe storage (8-10 C only for a few days), 1-3 weeks, chilling-sensitive below ~10 C. Respiration ~25-45 mW/kg at 10 C (ASHRAE Refrigeration Handbook, Commodity Storage Requirements). Q10 2.5 typical for produce (assumed).

leafy_greens.label: Leafy greens (spinach / lettuce)
leafy_greens.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (2016), Spinach: 0 C, 95-100 % RH, 10-14 days. Respiration ~20-30 mW/kg at 0 C (ASHRAE). Q10 ~3 for leafy vegetables (assumed, literature range 2-4).

grapes.label: Grapes (table)
grapes.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (2016), Grape: -1 to 0 C, 1-6 months depending on cultivar; 6 weeks used (conservative, no SO2 pads). Respiration ~3-7 mW/kg at 0 C (ASHRAE). Q10 3 assumed.

pomegranate.cp_source: University of Wisconsin crop-storage table 'Specific heat of fruits and vegetables' (adapted from ASHRAE / Engineering ToolBox): pomegranate 3.56 kJ/kg·K above freezing, 1.72 below. https://fyi.extension.wisc.edu/cropstorage/files/2019/09/Specific_heat_fruits-Vegetables.pdf
pomegranate.respiration_source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 values as reproduced by Pekmezci & Erkan (pomegranate chapter): 4–8 mg CO2/kg·h at 5 °C, 8–16 at 10 °C, 16–36 at 20 °C – check against the HB66 pomegranate page. Heat = mg CO2/kg·h × 2.96 mW/kg (HB66 conversion: × 61.2 kcal/t/day). Mid value at 5 °C: 6 × 2.96 = 17.8 mW/kg.

fruit.mass_source: E – assumption for counting (Bhagwa studies report about 285 g to 406 g per fruit; 250 g = small grade).
fruit.diameter_source: E – Bhagwa maturity study reports about 8.4 cm at harvest; commercial grades 7.5–8.5 cm.
fruit.fruit_density_source: E – whole fruit close to water (check: weigh + water displacement).
fruit.bulk_density_source: E – fruit loose in a crate, packing fraction about 0.55.

pomegranate.label: Pomegranate
pomegranate.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (2016), Pomegranate: 5 C, 90-95 % RH, 2-3 months; chilling injury below 5 C. Respiration: see respiration_source (HB66 4-8 mg CO2/kg.h at 5 C = 12-24 mW/kg; mid 17.8 mW/kg used; earlier value 8 mW/kg was too low). Q10 2.5 assumed.

freshness.T_opt_source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (2016), Pomegranate (Kader): best storage 5 °C, 90–95 % RH, up to 2 months.
freshness.T_freeze_source: USDA HB66 / ASHRAE Refrigeration Handbook (Commodity Storage Requirements): highest freezing point of pomegranate −3.0 °C.
freshness.damaged_source: E – assumption (example value from the project brief); no published single number. Edit here.
freshness.chill_source: E – assumption. Chilling injury below 5 °C is published (USDA HB66) but no rate coefficient; 0.15 /K² makes 1 h at 2 °C use 2.35 h of life (more than 1 h at 8 °C = 1.32 h). Edit here.
freshness.K_t_source: E – proxy. Pomegranate is not in the ASHRAE/Sastry et al. (1978) transpiration-coefficient table; the tomato value (140 mg kg⁻¹ s⁻¹ MPa⁻¹, same table) is used until measured. Weight-loss rate (%/h) = K_t × VPD(hPa) × 3.6e-5 × (v/1 m/s)^0.5.
freshness.WL_max_source: Kader (2002) Postharvest Technology of Horticultural Crops: most produce becomes unsaleable at 3–10 % weight loss; pomegranate shrivels visibly at about 5 % (chosen value, check).
freshness.status: Published values have a source; values marked E are assumptions to be checked/measured.

mango.label: Mango
mango.source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66 (2016), Mango: 13 C, 2-3 weeks; chilling injury below 10-13 C depending on cultivar (12 C used). Respiration ~50-90 mW/kg at 13 C (ASHRAE). Q10 2.5 assumed. NOTE: our 2-8 C room is too cold for mango - the site will warn.

milk.label: Milk (pasteurised, packed)
milk.source: FSSAI / typical dairy practice: pasteurised milk at or below 4 C, about 7-14 days; 10 days used. Spoilage Q10 ~3 for psychrotrophic bacteria (assumed). Not a living product, so no respiration heat.

vaccines.label: Vaccines (VVM30 class, illustrative)
vaccines.source: WHO: store at +2 to +8 C, do not freeze. VVM30 category = end point after 30 days at 37 C or 4 years at 5 C (WHO PQS E006/IN05). Q10 derived from those two points: (1460/30)^(10/32) = 3.37. Illustrative only - real vaccines follow their own VVM.

jasmine.label: Jasmine (malle, loose buds)
jasmine.best_storage_source: E – ICAR-IARI review 2025 (crop-calendar research); check the paper.
jasmine.fit_note: Best range is 4-7 °C. Fragrance fades before the look does.
jasmine.rh_source: USDA Agriculture Handbook 66: 90-95 % RH for most cut flowers.
jasmine.shelf_life_ambient_source: E – ambient 12-30 h (mid 21 h); crop-calendar research; Jawaharlal et al. 2012.
jasmine.shelf_life_bagged_source: E – 18 days white buds / 12 days fragrance in 0.03 mm PE at 2-5 C; 7 days in 60 micron PE + 4 % boric acid at 7 C (crop-calendar research; Singh et al. 2009, ISHS Acta Hort. 847).
jasmine.Q10_source: C – from the two shelf lives: (18.0/0.875)^(10/(30-4)) = 3.2. Freshness reaches 0 at the reference shelf life in both cases.
jasmine.respiration_source: E – no species table found. Class value for cut flowers: 40-60 mg CO2/kg.h at 5 C ('very high' class, Kader / UC Davis); mid 50. Other temperatures from Q10 = 2.6 (cut snapdragons 0-20 C, ISHS Acta Hort. 628). Heat = mg CO2/kg.h x 2.96 mW/kg (USDA Handbook 66 conversion).
jasmine.cp_source: C – Siebel's rule cp = 0.837 + 3.349 x water fraction (0.82, E typical).
jasmine.kg_per_crate_source: E – loose flowers in a 600 x 400 x 300 mm ventilated crate, not pressed (design brief / our estimate).
jasmine.bulk_density_source: C – kg per crate / inside volume of the crate (0.056 m3).
jasmine.ethylene_source: E – buds open and brown faster with ethylene (check).
jasmine.chill_source: E – no injury at 2 C in film (Singh et al. 2009); flag below 2 C.
jasmine.boric_source: E – 4 % boric acid dip, about 2x life (jasmine in 60 micron PE at 7 C: 7 days; crop-calendar research).
jasmine.price_source: E – Visakhapatnam press reports (Deccan Chronicle, Anandapuram market / rythu bazaars 2023-2025). Prices swing a lot; check before use.

freshness.K_t_source: E – set so loose, unbagged flowers at 30 C, 70 % RH lose about 7 % of weight a day.
freshness.WL_max_source: E – unbagged flowers are hard to sell after about 15 % weight loss. With a PE bag there is no water-loss penalty (the bagged shelf life already includes it).

fragrance.note: Fragrance ends before looks: 12 days of fragrance against 18 days of white buds (0.03 mm PE, 2-5 C). The fragrance score runs 18/12 = 1.5x faster.
fragrance.source: E – crop-calendar research (jasmine in 0.03 mm PE at 2-5 C).

jasmine.plan_hold_source: E – the season plan never holds a flower longer than this (about a quarter of its bagged shelf life at 4 C, so most of the freshness is still there at sale).

blocked_flowers._about: Flowers that must NOT go into the 4 C room. Check-in refuses them.

anthurium.label: Anthurium
anthurium.warning: Anthurium needs 10–13 °C or warmer. At 4 °C it gets chilling injury (purple, then brown). Do not store it in this room.
anthurium.source: UC Davis Postharvest (Anthurium): store at 12.5-20 C; below 10 C causes purpling, browning and death.

orchid.label: Orchids (tropical)
orchid.warning: Tropical orchids need 10–13 °C. At 4 °C they get chilling injury. Do not store them in this room.
orchid.source: E – design brief; USDA Handbook 66 lists most tropical orchids at 7-13 C (check).

flower_rules.ethylene: No fruit in the room. Ripening fruit (banana, mango, tomato, papaya) gives off ethylene gas, which makes flowers open, drop petals and brown early.
flower_rules.ethylene_source: UC Davis Postharvest; USDA Agriculture Handbook 66.
flower_rules.water: Never spray water directly on the flowers: wet petals rot. Raise the room humidity instead (bags, fogger).
handling: Pick at bud stage, early in the morning.
Optional boric-acid dip (jasmine, tuberose) – about 2× life (E).
Keep the door closed at night.

faq_months.q: Can flowers be stored for months?
faq_months.a: No. Fresh loose flowers last 1–3 weeks at best (bagged, 2–7 °C). Only carnation buds at 0–1 °C with special treatment can last months. Our room is a 1–7 day holding room. For long-term value: jasmine concrete, marigold lutein/dye, rose gulkand, dried flowers.
